metadata.title: Why Elon Musk's track record of unfilled promises matters for investors

content.text:
00:00 Speaker A
SpaceX is preparing for what could be the biggest IPO in history, but a lingering question for investors is how much weight should they put on Elon Musk's promises. Analysis from the New York Times examines more than 600 goals Musk laid out over the past 15 years, found a mixed record when it comes to delivering. Joining us now is New York Times investigative business reporter, Kristin Grind, one of the reporters behind that analysis. All right, Kristen, so your story says Musk hit only about 19% of his goals on time.
00:40 Kristin Grind
We follow all of these things he's saying on X and in earnings calls. You know, he's going to the Mars, he's going to Mars, he's launching autonomous vehicles, and we really wanted to understand how much he's followed through on all of that over the years. So we built this database starting in 2011, looking at all the statements he's made with a goal and a defined timeline. And then we spent months researching what happened after he said this. Did he follow through? Did these promises come true? What happened? And essentially, we found that his track record is pretty poor.
01:31 Speaker A
Some might push back and say, and I'm interested to get your take on this. They might say, you know, at the end of the day, Christian, why does this matter?
01:39 Kristin Grind
A lot of um Musk investors and and even some employees believe he says these things and says these promises just to kind of get them going and working harder towards a goal. So they're kind of forgiving of him in that way. It's a very big deal though to understand how much he is following through and delivering on this. A bet on any of his companies and with the SpaceX IPO coming up, you know, just this week is a bet on Elon Musk. And as an investor, you need to know when he says Tesla is going to be driving autonomous vehicles in two years and you're putting your money in the market on that, is that really going to come true?
02:30 Speaker A
Could you care I mean, we've known this guy for a long time. You've been reporting on him for a long time. I've been talking about him for a long time. Don't you think at this point in some sense, Kristen, I mean, investors kind of know and and they're they're kind of discounting his timelines?
02:49 Kristin Grind
So, you may know this, but in Tesla, and we'll see how it ends up in SpaceX, there are a lot of small investors in that company. So investors who are not like your big asset managers or your your venture capitalists or people who really know what they're doing. And these are people that are not paying attention quite as much as me or you or an institutional asset manager. And so I think even after all this time, it's really important for those types of investors to understand what they're getting into at any of these Musk companies.
03:31 Kristin Grind
Let's take a real world example. Elon is saying he's now going to build AI data centers in space. If I was going to invest in SpaceX, I would say, what has been his main goal at SpaceX literally since its founding in 2002. It's been to get to Mars. That has been his whole business proposition. It's trickled down to all his other businesses and over the years, he has continued to hammer on that. We're getting to Mars, we're going to colonize Mars. Every few years he's changed that timeline, pushed it out, said different things about what's going to happen. And here we are in 2026 and suddenly he's saying, actually it's going to be another 20 years for Mars. Now we're going to colonize the moon, which is something he had never planned to do his entire career. So, if I'm going to bet on SpaceX, I would definitely want to know that history. So when I'm thinking about his promise to build AI data centers in space, for example, I can then think, well, how did other promises pan out before that?
